source.title: MoGU V2: Toward a Higher Pareto Frontier Between Model Usability and Security
source.authors: Yan-Rui Du; Feng-Lei Fan; Sen-Dong Zhao; Jia-Wei Cao; Ting Liu; Bing Qin

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether benign instruction fine-tuning affects harmful-response behavior and evaluates jailbreak attack outcomes, using its own training data and security measures rather than reproducing the original studies’ methods.
record.gate_note: The study reports harmfulness scores and attack-success rates before and after benign task fine-tuning, plus attack-suite rates on several base models. The attack rates aggregate different prompts and do not isolate the effect of a compliant opening, suffix, or decoding change. Excluded results include router-weight distributions, layer-wise classifier performance, MoGU security results, ablations, and usability/task-performance measures because they do not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: A defense paper (MoGUv2) that still reports how much benign instruction fine-tuning raises harmfulness. LoRA IFT on UltraInteract plus Alpaca raises GPT-judge HS and ASR on Llama2-7B and Qwen2-7B (Table VII), which bears on V2 with a different recipe than the originals. Its appendix per-attack ASRs for base models (Tables XII–XIII) include a compliant-opening prompt (Comp.) and a GCG suffix next to plain AdvBench requests, which bears weakly on V4. Everything else is the authors' own method's performance.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that routing between glad and unwilling LoRA variants (MoGUv2) improves security across mainstream, on-device and reasoning LLMs while preserving usability. They also conclude that, with a data-mix strategy, MoGUv2 restores or exceeds base-model security after instruction fine-tuning while keeping task gains. The 5-token decoding is an inference setting, not a conclusion.
record.recipe_differences: Tests benign downstream instruction fine-tuning with 6,659 UltraInteract and 10,000 Alpaca samples, plus a combined jailbreak benchmark; it does not reproduce the original harmful-example fine-tuning or token-level KL analysis.
record.method_sensitivity: IFT effects are reported for two models and one mixed task/dialogue dataset; the attack-suite ASR varies across models. The study also evaluates different attack types, but the aggregate ASRs do not isolate their individual effects.

fits_no_version.finding: A router-based defense applied only to the first 5 decoded tokens, with the base model generating the rest, cuts aggregate ASR sharply (e.g. Vicuna 38.29%→2.79%, Falcon 61.77%→6.56%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Intervening only on the opening tokens is enough to restore refusal in most cases, consistent with safety being decided at the opening.

fits_no_version.finding: Linear probes separate benign from malicious instructions best in later layers. Routers placed in the latter half of layers outperform early-half placement (e.g. Falcon 9.10% vs 50.14% ASR).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety-relevant representations concentrate in deeper layers.

record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The benign IFT result uses a mixed task-specific and general dialogue dataset, so it does not isolate ordinary benign data alone. Attack-suite ASRs aggregate several prompt sets and attacks, preventing attribution to compliant openings, suffixes, or decoding changes individually.
record.rows_left_out: MoGU and MoGUv2 security comparisons, router-weight distributions, layer probes, early-versus-latter-layer comparisons, ablations, usability scores, and task-performance scores were not included because they do not directly measure the specified claim versions. Attack-specific rates were not extracted where the appendix table layout did not support unambiguous assignment; aggregate ASRs are recorded instead.

untested.parts: Small benign sets (few to a few hundred examples); full fine-tuning (only LoRA used); benign data without the reasoning-task mix.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models.
True prefilling of the response, decoding changes, and matched with/without-opening comparisons on the same prompts. Comp. is a prompt instruction, not a prefill.
No weight- or rank-level localization. The layer probe concerns hidden-state separability, not parameters.
No training that spreads safety beyond the first tokens. MoGUv2 acts only on the first 5 tokens.

missing.what: Per-benchmark HS after IFT on plain harmful requests (Adv. and CatQA) versus jailbreak sets: Llama Adv 1.04→2.06, Cat 1.00→1.79; Qwen Adv 1.04→2.33, Cat 1.41→2.53.
Per-attack base-model ASR for Comp. (compliant opening) and GCG (suffix) next to plain AdvBench, for all 11 models.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a defense paper. The IFT setup follows the authors' prior work (arXiv:2410.04524). The aggregate V4 rows should be replaced with per-attack rows. No uncertainty estimates are reported.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning intervention is tested for its effect on naturally arising harmful compliance.
Does not test fine-tuning on only a few to a few hundred benign examples, or isolate ordinary benign data from the task-specific data mixture. Measures HS and ASR rather than refusal removal itself.
No per-token KL divergence comparison between aligned and base models.

The security evaluation includes jailbreak attacks and reports aggregate ASR, but does not report matched comparisons isolating compliant prefills, suffixes, or decoding changes, nor test each mechanism separately.
Does not test whether a small set of model weights or ranks carries safety behavior.
Does not test why safety behavior is shallow or whether data or training objectives cause that property.
Does not test training that spreads safety across response positions or whether such training holds up.
